Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes): Right knee pain with clicking for ~2 weeks after increasing running mileage while training for a marathon. Pain typically begins ~20 minutes into a run (~2.5–3 miles). Transient mild swelling after first long run resolved with ice. One episode of transient tingling in right toes after a run. Prior fall during ice hockey months ago with large bruise. No chronic diseases documented.  
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes): Not recorded.  
- Current medications including OTC and traditional medicines: Ibuprofen — patient reports ~400 mg max sometimes; dose/route/frequency not documented. Aleve (patient stated; class/confirmation uncertain) — dose/route/frequency not documented. Vitamin D — dose/route/frequency not documented. Melatonin — dose/route/frequency not documented. Xanax (occasional use) — dose/route/frequency not documented. Occasional cannabis use (smokes a joint) — dose/route/frequency not documented.  
- Immunisation status reviewed (flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal, shingles, tetanus): Not recorded.  
- Sexual/reproductive health status and risks: Not recorded.  
- Lifestyle: physical activity, diet, tobacco, alcohol, substance use: Actively training for a marathon; running sessions include 4–8 mile runs, long runs started ~1 month ago; attends gym a few times per week; plays ice hockey. Occasional cannabis use. No tobacco or alcohol use recorded. Diet not recorded.  
- Hearing and vision concerns: Far-sighted; history of LASIK surgery. Hearing concerns not recorded.  
- Mood, mental health, and risk assessment (depression, anxiety, self-harm): Occasional use of Xanax for sleep/stress reported. No other mental health issues, depressive symptoms, anxiety, or self-harm risk documented.  
- Social context: family support, caregiving, housing, financial stressors: Lives in London; home address provided. Active in community/sports. No caregiving, housing or financial stressors recorded.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings and impression:
  - Right anterior/medial-to-lateral knee pain with audible/subjective clicking during flexion/extension and activity for ~2 weeks after increasing running mileage.  
  - Pain onset during runs (~20 minutes in), aggravated by running and certain gym movements (straightening from flexion).  
  - Transient mild swelling after the first long run resolved with ice; currently no visible swelling, no warmth, full range of motion, no locking, no giving-way reported, able to walk and use stairs.  
  - One transient episode of right toe tingling after a run that has since resolved.
- Working diagnosis (supported by transcript and DDx): Patellofemoral pain syndrome / patellar maltracking (runner’s knee) — high likelihood given recent mileage increase, anterior knee pain provoked by running, clicking with flexion/extension, and transient exercise-related swelling.  
- Relevant differentials from DDx that refine the assessment:
  - Iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome — medium likelihood; timing of pain partway through runs and lateral component of pain reported support this.  
  - Meniscal or intra-articular cartilage injury (post-traumatic or degenerative) — medium likelihood; prior hockey fall and intermittent clicking could reflect a small meniscal/chondral lesion, though absence of locking or focal joint-line tenderness lowers likelihood.
- Considerations (additional plausible but uncertain options from DDx):
  - Patellar tendinopathy / bursitis — possible with overuse and activity-related pain.  
  - Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) — low likelihood (absence of persistent calf pain, warmth, erythema or systemic features) but considered given intermittent swelling; clinical features do not support it presently.  
  - Peripheral nerve irritation (exertional neurapraxia) — possible explanation for the single episode of toe tingling.
- Management plan documented in transcript:
  - Conservative measures advised: continue ice therapy and reduce running mileage; avoid running through pain.  
  - Pharmacologic: patient offered a stronger anti-inflammatory prescription to be sent to pharmacy; counsel to take with food and not to co-administer with other NSAIDs (patient told not to take it together with ibuprofen). (Medication name/dose not documented in transcript.)  
  - Referral: referral to physiotherapy arranged as initial assessment and management. Physiotherapist assessment to determine need for imaging.  
  - Safety netting: urgent review recommended if persistent swelling, increasing heat/redness, fever, systemic unwellness, or inability to bend/straighten the knee (locking) — seek urgent medical attention in those cases.  
  - Imaging: not performed at this visit; imaging (e.g., X-ray/MRI) to be considered if symptoms persist or on physiotherapy/clinical review.
- Conflicts or uncertainties: None identified between transcript and DDx. Lack of in-person physical examination limits diagnostic certainty.

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification: Advised specific knee care measures — ice therapy, reduce running mileage, avoid running through pain; counsel regarding NSAID use and taking anti-inflammatories with food. No broader chronic disease prevention education documented.  
- Patient health goals and priorities: Training for a marathon in June; primary goal is to continue training while addressing knee pain.  
- Eligibility for GP Management Plan (GPMP) or Team Care Arrangements (TCA): Not recorded.  
- Referrals (allied health, Quitline, AOD services, Aboriginal health worker, or social supports): Physiotherapy referral to be sent; prescription to pharmacy for a stronger anti-inflammatory to be sent. Possible clinic appointment with doctor if physiotherapy wait is long or if symptoms worsen.  
- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled: No scheduled follow-up documented; patient instructed to seek urgent review for red-flag symptoms; clinician offered clinic review if needed.

Consider

- Mental health support or counselling referral: Not recorded (occasional Xanax for sleep noted).  
- Specialist referral for complex chronic disease management: Specialist (orthopedics/sports medicine/imaging) referral considered if symptoms persist, mechanical symptoms develop, or if imaging/intervention required.  
- Dental referral if oral health issues identified: Not recorded.  
- Optometry referral for visual concerns or regular screening: Not recorded (history of LASIK only).  
- Audiometry referral if hearing issues suspected: Not recorded.  
- Social work or housing support referral if social determinants affect health: Not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Patellofemoral pain syndrome (runner's knee) — High likelihood. Justification: Recent increase in running mileage, anterior knee pain starting after ~20 minutes of running, clicking with flexion/extension, and transient exertional swelling improved with ice.  
- Iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome / lateral overuse tendinopathy — Medium likelihood. Justification: Pain onset partway through runs and report of pain shifting laterally on the right are consistent with ITB friction syndrome in runners.  
- Meniscal or intra-articular cartilage injury (post-traumatic or degenerative) — Medium likelihood. Justification: Intermittent clicking and prior hockey fall could reflect a meniscal or chondral lesion becoming symptomatic with increased load; absence of locking or focal joint-line tenderness reduces but does not exclude likelihood.

Quality checks

- Missing but clinically expected elements: No recorded vital signs (BP/pulse/temperature), no anthropometric data (height/weight/BMI), no documented focused knee physical exam findings (palpation, focal tenderness, ligament testing), no imaging performed or ordered at time of consultation, no documented immunization review, and no baseline blood tests or chronic disease screening documented.  
- Internal conflicts or contradictions between transcript and DDx: None identified.  
- Transcript quality notes: Video consultation; patient sometimes uncertain about medication names/classes (Aleve vs acetaminophen), and switched between miles/kilometers when describing distances. Physical examination limited by video format and lack of in-person palpation — clinical assessment and diagnosis are therefore limited pending physiotherapy/in-person assessment.
